investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: On nerve conduction studies, what is the hallmark of an AXONAL neuropathy?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: Reduced CMAP/SNAP amplitude with relatively preserved conduction velocity (amplitude reflects the number of surviving axons).

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: On nerve conduction studies, what is the hallmark of a DEMYELINATING neuropathy?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: Slowed conduction velocity, prolonged distal latency, conduction block and temporal dispersion, with amplitude relatively preserved (e.g. GBS, CIDP, CMT1).

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: How long after an acute nerve injury do denervation changes (fibrillations, positive sharp waves) appear on needle EMG?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: About 2–3 weeks, so an EMG done too early can be falsely normal.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: What EMG findings distinguish a myopathic from a neuropathic motor unit pattern?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: Myopathic: small, short-duration, polyphasic units with early/full recruitment. Neuropathic (chronic/reinnervated): large, long-duration, polyphasic units with reduced recruitment.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: What neurophysiology pattern suggests motor neurone disease?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: Widespread active denervation with fibrillations and fasciculations across multiple regions, combined with normal sensory nerve action potentials (anterior horn cell disease).

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: What RNS pattern is characteristic of myasthenia gravis, and at what stimulation frequency?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: A decremental CMAP response (>10% drop between 1st and 4th/5th response) on LOW-frequency repetitive stimulation at 2–3 Hz, reflecting a postsynaptic AChR antibody defect.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: What RNS pattern is characteristic of LEMS?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: A small resting CMAP that shows an incremental response (facilitation, typically ≥60–100% increment) after high-frequency stimulation (20–50 Hz) or ~10 seconds of maximal voluntary exercise, reflecting a presynaptic VGCC antibody defect.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: Which antibody and NMJ location underlie MG versus LEMS?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: MG: postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies (or MuSK). LEMS: presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC) antibodies, often paraneoplastic with small-cell lung cancer.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: What is the most sensitive electrophysiological test for an NMJ disorder, and what is its limitation?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: Single-fibre EMG, which shows increased jitter (+/- blocking). It is the most sensitive test but is not specific, as increased jitter occurs in other neuromuscular diseases.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: How does muscle strength change with repeated activity in MG versus LEMS?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: MG: weakness worsens with use (fatigable). LEMS: strength transiently improves with brief exercise (facilitation), mirroring the increment seen on high-frequency RNS.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: What does single-fibre EMG (SFEMG) measure?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: Jitter — the variability in the time interval between the firing of two muscle fibres belonging to the same motor unit — and, in more severe defects, blocking (intermittent failure of a fibre to fire).

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: Why is jitter increased in myasthenia gravis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: A reduced safety factor of NMJ transmission means the endplate potential reaches firing threshold with variable delay from discharge to discharge, increasing the timing variability (jitter); complete failures produce blocking.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: How does the sensitivity of SFEMG compare with RNS and antibodies in MG?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: SFEMG is the most sensitive test (>95% in an appropriate muscle) and can be abnormal even when repetitive nerve stimulation is normal and AChR antibodies are negative, e.g. in ocular or seronegative MG.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: What is the key limitation of SFEMG?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: It is highly sensitive but non-specific: increased jitter also occurs in LEMS, botulism, motor neurone disease, neuropathies, myopathies and reinnervation, so it must be interpreted with the clinical picture and antibodies.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: Which muscles are commonly studied with SFEMG and what preparation is needed?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: Extensor digitorum communis (limb) and frontalis/orbicularis oculi (ocular disease); cholinesterase inhibitors such as pyridostigmine are usually withheld beforehand so they do not mask abnormal transmission.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: What does the VEP P100 latency measure?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: The time for the cortical (occipital) response to appear after a pattern-reversal visual stimulus, reflecting conduction speed through the visual pathway — chiefly the optic nerve. Normal latency is around 100 ms.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: What VEP pattern indicates optic nerve demyelination?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: A DELAYED P100 latency with PRESERVED amplitude. Demyelination slows conduction (delays the wave) while the axons — and therefore amplitude — remain relatively intact.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: Why is a delayed VEP useful in suspected multiple sclerosis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: It gives objective evidence of a previous or subclinical episode of optic neuritis, revealing a second lesion and supporting dissemination in space even when acuity and fundoscopy are normal.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: How do you distinguish demyelination from axonal loss on VEP?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: Demyelination delays latency with preserved amplitude; axonal loss (e.g. ischaemic or compressive optic neuropathy) reduces amplitude with relatively preserved latency.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: Is a delayed VEP specific to multiple sclerosis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: No. It indicates optic nerve demyelination but occurs in other optic neuropathies, compressive and hereditary conditions. It supports but cannot alone diagnose MS.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: What EEG pattern is characteristic of childhood absence epilepsy?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: Generalised, symmetrical 3Hz spike-and-wave discharges, classically provoked by hyperventilation.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: Which EEG finding supports herpes simplex (HSV) encephalitis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: Periodic lateralised epileptiform discharges (PLEDs) over the temporal lobe(s), reflecting temporal-lobe involvement.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: What EEG abnormality is associated with sporadic CJD?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: Periodic sharp-wave complexes at roughly 1Hz.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: What is the classic EEG pattern in West syndrome (infantile spasms)?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: Hypsarrhythmia — chaotic, high-amplitude, disorganised background with multifocal spikes.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: Does a normal routine EEG exclude epilepsy?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: No. Routine interictal EEG has limited sensitivity (~30–50%); epilepsy is a clinical diagnosis supported by EEG, and a normal study does not rule it out. EEG also has no role in diagnosing syncope.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: Median neuropathy at the wrist is confirmed on NCS — what is the management ladder?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: Nocturnal wrist splint → corticosteroid injection → surgical decompression for severe/refractory disease (thenar wasting, denervation). Screen for secondary causes: hypothyroidism, pregnancy, acromegaly, RA, diabetes.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: A demyelinating polyneuropathy on NCS suggests GBS — how is it managed?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: IVIG or plasma exchange; corticosteroids do NOT help in GBS. Monitor serial FVC for respiratory failure (ITU/ventilation) and give VTE prophylaxis. A chronic, relapsing, steroid-responsive form is CIDP.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.front: Once decremental RNS confirms myasthenia gravis, what two next steps follow?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.back: Send anti-AChR (then anti-MuSK if negative) and image the thymus (CT/MRI mediastinum) for thymoma (~10–15%, resectable).

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What are the normal CSF values for protein, glucose and cell count?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back:
• Protein 0.15–0.45 g/L
  • glucose ~2/3 (60–70%) of serum glucose
  • fewer than 5 cells/mm3 with no neutrophils.
A paired serum glucose must always be taken to interpret the CSF glucose.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: Classic CSF pattern of bacterial (pyogenic) meningitis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back:
• Turbid fluid
  • high neutrophils/polymorphs
  • high protein (>1 g/L)
  • and low glucose (<50% of serum).
The low glucose ratio and neutrophilia are the key discriminators.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: How does viral meningitis CSF differ from bacterial?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Viral: clear fluid, lymphocyte predominance, mildly raised protein (<1 g/L) and NORMAL glucose. Bacterial has neutrophils and low glucose.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: CSF findings in TB or fungal meningitis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Lymphocyte predominance, very high protein (often 1–5 g/L, may form a fibrin web), and very low glucose. Glucose distinguishes it from viral, which has normal glucose.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: Should you delay antibiotics to perform the LP in suspected bacterial meningitis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: No. Give empirical IV antibiotics (and steroids per NICE) immediately; never delay treatment for the tap or its results. Treat first and perform the LP once safe if it must be deferred for CT.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What pigment causes CSF xanthochromia and why is it specific for SAH?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Bilirubin, produced when red cells are broken down and haemoglobin is metabolised in vivo by macrophages. Because this enzymatic conversion cannot happen in a test tube, its presence confirms blood was in the subarachnoid space rather than introduced by the needle.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: How long after headache onset should the LP be performed to detect xanthochromia?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: At least 12 hours after onset, allowing time for oxyhaemoglobin to be converted to bilirubin. An LP done earlier may be falsely negative.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: How does a traumatic tap differ from true SAH on CSF analysis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: In a traumatic tap the red-cell count falls between the first and last collection bottles and there is no xanthochromia. In true SAH the red-cell count is constant across bottles and bilirubin/xanthochromia is present.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: Why is spectrophotometry preferred over visual inspection of the supernatant?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Spectrophotometry measures net bilirubin absorbance across the visible spectrum, detecting small amounts and distinguishing it from oxyhaemoglobin, jaundice or high protein. Visual inspection is insensitive and unreliable.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What is the role of CT before LP in suspected SAH?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: A normal non-contrast CT within 6 hours of headache onset, reported by an experienced clinician, largely excludes SAH. Beyond 6 hours, or if CT is negative but suspicion persists, an LP for xanthochromia is required.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What laboratory technique is used to detect CSF oligoclonal bands?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Isoelectric focusing (IEF) of CSF followed by IgG-specific immunofixation/immunoblotting, run on paired CSF and serum samples. IEF separates immunoglobulins by isoelectric point and is more sensitive than older agarose electrophoresis.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: Which oligoclonal band pattern supports multiple sclerosis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Two or more bands present in the CSF but absent from the paired serum (CSF-restricted bands), indicating intrathecal IgG synthesis. Identical bands in both CSF and serum (mirror pattern) reflect a systemic process and do NOT support MS.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: How is the IgG index calculated and what value indicates intrathecal synthesis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: IgG index = (CSF IgG / serum IgG) divided by (CSF albumin / serum albumin). A value greater than 0.7 indicates raised intrathecal IgG production while correcting for blood-brain barrier integrity.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: In the McDonald criteria, what role can CSF-specific oligoclonal bands play?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: In a patient with a clinically isolated syndrome, the presence of CSF-specific oligoclonal bands can substitute for the requirement to demonstrate dissemination in time, allowing an earlier diagnosis of MS.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: Besides MS, name conditions that can produce CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands.
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back:
• CNS infections (neurosyphilis, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, HIV, chronic viral encephalitis)
  • neurosarcoidosis
  • and CNS involvement of systemic autoimmune disease such as SLE.
OCBs indicate CNS inflammation, not MS specifically.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What is the classic CSF finding in Guillain-Barré syndrome?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Albuminocytological dissociation — raised CSF protein (>0.45 g/L) with a normal white cell count (≤5 cells/mm³).

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: Why can the CSF be normal in the first week of GBS?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: CSF protein typically rises only after ~1–2 weeks. A normal early result does not exclude GBS; if suspicion is high, treat and consider repeating the LP.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What CSF finding argues AGAINST GBS, and what should you consider?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: A raised cell count (pleocytosis, >10 cells/mm³). Consider infection, malignant meningitis, or HIV seroconversion instead.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What are the three diagnostic pillars of GBS?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back:
• 1) Clinical: ascending weakness with areflexia, often post-infection.
  • 2) CSF: albuminocytological dissociation.
  • 3) Nerve conduction studies: demyelinating pattern.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: How is GBS monitored and treated, and what must be avoided?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Monitor FVC serially for respiratory failure and watch for autonomic instability. Treat with IVIG or plasma exchange. Corticosteroids are NOT effective.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What is the normal range for CSF opening pressure at LP in an adult?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: 6–20 cmH₂O (values up to ~25 cmH₂O may be accepted as borderline); measured in the lateral decubitus position with a manometer.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What opening pressure defines idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: >25 cmH₂O with normal brain imaging and normal CSF constituents, typically in an obese young woman with headache, papilloedema and visual loss.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: Why must opening pressure be measured in the lateral decubitus (not sitting) position?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Sitting adds a hydrostatic column that falsely elevates the reading; a reliable value requires the patient lying laterally with the manometer zeroed at the needle and the patient relaxed.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: How does the tap help diagnose normal-pressure hydrocephalus (NPH)?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Opening pressure is normal; removing a large volume of CSF (~30–50 mL) and seeing objective gait improvement predicts a good response to shunting. The triad is gait apraxia, dementia and urinary incontinence.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: When is LP to measure opening pressure contraindicated?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: When raised ICP is due to a suspected mass lesion or there are focal neurological signs/reduced GCS — draining CSF risks tonsillar herniation (coning). Image the brain first.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: A febrile, confused patient has a lymphocytic CSF — what must you do?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Suspect HSV encephalitis: send CSF HSV PCR and start empirical IV aciclovir immediately, before the result returns (untreated HSV encephalitis has ~70% mortality).

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What is the empirical treatment for a bacterial CSF picture?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: IV ceftriaxone (add amoxicillin if ≥60, immunocompromised or pregnant, for Listeria) + IV dexamethasone; blood cultures + meningococcal PCR. Do NOT delay antibiotics for the LP; meningococcal/bacterial meningitis is notifiable.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: Xanthochromia confirms subarachnoid haemorrhage — what are the next steps?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: CT angiography to localise the aneurysm and urgent neurosurgery/interventional referral; start nimodipine to reduce vasospasm.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What does a positive CSF 14-3-3 protein indicate, and why is it non-specific?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: It reflects rapid neuronal destruction with release of intraneuronal 14-3-3 into CSF. It is non-specific because it is also raised in stroke, viral encephalitis, hypoxia and status epilepticus — not just CJD.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What is RT-QuIC and what makes it valuable in CJD diagnosis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Real-time quaking-induced conversion: patient CSF seeds misfolding of recombinant prion substrate under cyclical shaking, detected by thioflavin T fluorescence. It is highly specific (>98%) for CJD and is now a diagnostic criterion for probable sporadic CJD.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What are the classic clinical features of sporadic CJD?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back:
• Rapidly progressive dementia over weeks to months
  • myoclonus (often startle-induced)
  • and additional cerebellar, visual or pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs.
It is invariably fatal, usually within months.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What are the characteristic EEG and MRI findings in sporadic CJD?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: EEG: periodic sharp-wave complexes at roughly 1 Hz. MRI DWI: cortical 'ribboning' hyperintensity and restricted diffusion in the caudate/putamen (basal ganglia); a pulvinar (thalamic) sign favours variant CJD.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: Why must special precautions be taken with instruments and CSF in suspected CJD?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: CJD is transmissible and prions resist standard sterilisation, autoclaving and formalin. Use single-use instruments where possible, quarantine or incinerate reusable ones per national prion guidance, and label CSF as high-risk.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What is the definitive/confirmatory test for herpes simplex encephalitis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: CSF HSV DNA PCR — high sensitivity (~96%) and specificity (~99%). It has replaced brain biopsy as the gold standard.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: Which organism and brain region typify herpes simplex encephalitis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: HSV-1 (usually), with predilection for the temporal and inferior frontal lobes, producing temporal-lobe MRI changes and clinical dysphasia/memory/personality change.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What is the key limitation of CSF HSV PCR in the first 24–72 hours?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: It may be falsely negative early because viral DNA is not yet detectable. A negative early PCR does not exclude HSE — continue aciclovir and repeat the PCR.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What is the typical CSF profile in HSV encephalitis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Lymphocytic pleocytosis (often 10–500 cells), raised protein, normal glucose; red cells may be present due to haemorrhagic necrosis.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: When should IV aciclovir be started in suspected HSV encephalitis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Immediately on clinical suspicion, before and regardless of PCR or imaging results. Delay increases mortality and disability; untreated mortality is around 70%.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What CSF orexin-A (hypocretin-1) level is diagnostic of narcolepsy type 1?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: ≤ 110 pg/mL (or less than one-third of the normal mean) measured against the standardised reference assay.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: Which neurons are lost in narcolepsy type 1, and by what mechanism?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Orexin (hypocretin)-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, destroyed by an autoimmune process strongly linked to HLA-DQB1*06:02.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What distinguishes narcolepsy type 1 from type 2 biochemically and clinically?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Type 1 has low/undetectable CSF orexin and cataplexy; type 2 has preserved orexin and no cataplexy.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: What are the MSLT criteria supporting narcolepsy?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Mean sleep latency ≤ 8 minutes plus ≥ 2 sleep-onset REM periods (following overnight polysomnography).

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: Name the REM-dissociation symptoms seen in narcolepsy besides cataplexy.
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Sleep paralysis and hypnagogic (sleep-onset) hallucinations, along with excessive daytime sleepiness.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: Narcolepsy type 1 is confirmed (low CSF orexin) — what are the next steps?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: Refer to sleep medicine; sleep hygiene + scheduled naps, modafinil for excessive daytime sleepiness and sodium oxybate for cataplexy. Safety: advise not to drive and to notify the DVLA until symptoms are controlled.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.front: A positive RT-QuIC confirms probable CJD — what follows?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.back: There is no cure: supportive/palliative care with MDT input, maintain prion precautions (single-use or quarantined instruments) and notify the national CJD surveillance unit. Definitive diagnosis is neuropathological.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: A patient with a length-dependent sensory neuropathy has nerve conduction studies showing markedly reduced sensory and motor amplitudes but conduction velocities that are only mildly reduced and remain above 80% of normal. Which process does this pattern indicate?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: Amplitude reflects the number of functioning axons, so reduced CMAP/SNAP amplitude with preserved velocity is the signature of axon loss. Demyelination instead produces slowed velocity and prolonged latency.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: A 24-year-old develops ascending weakness over several days. Nerve conduction studies show prolonged distal latencies, slowed conduction velocities, conduction block and prolonged/absent F-waves. Which diagnosis do these findings best support?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: Slowed velocity, prolonged latency, conduction block and early F-wave abnormalities define an acquired demyelinating polyneuropathy, characteristic of GBS. F-wave changes are among the earliest findings because they test the proximal nerve segments and roots.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: During needle EMG on a patient taking warfarin, which precaution is most important?
options: Cool the limb below 30°C before inserting the needle
Limit sampling to avoid deep muscles and account for the bleeding risk from coagulopathy
Perform the study only within 24 hours of symptom onset
Avoid all sensory nerve conduction studies
Give a prophylactic dose of neuromuscular blocker
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.answer: Limit sampling to avoid deep muscles and account for the bleeding risk from coagulopathy
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: Needle EMG penetrates muscle and can cause haematoma in anticoagulated patients, so the study is planned carefully with limited, superficial muscle sampling and attention to the INR. Cooling the limb would spuriously slow conduction and is never done deliberately.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: A 40-year-old woman with fatigable ptosis and diplopia undergoes repetitive nerve stimulation. Which finding best supports a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis?
options: An increment of more than 60% after high-frequency stimulation
A small resting CMAP that facilitates after exercise
A decrement of more than 10% in CMAP amplitude on 2–3 Hz stimulation
Fibrillation potentials at rest on needle EMG
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.answer: A decrement of more than 10% in CMAP amplitude on 2–3 Hz stimulation
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: MG is a postsynaptic AChR antibody disorder with a low safety factor, so repeated low-frequency stimulation depletes ACh and produces a decremental response exceeding 10%. This decrement on 2–3 Hz stimulation is the classic RNS signature of myasthenia gravis.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: A 62-year-old smoker has proximal weakness that improves briefly after exertion. RNS shows a small resting CMAP with a marked increment after 10 seconds of exercise. What is the most important next investigation?
options: CT of the chest to look for small-cell lung cancer
Nerve conduction studies of sensory nerves
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.answer: CT of the chest to look for small-cell lung cancer
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: The incremental (facilitation) pattern with a small resting CMAP is diagnostic of LEMS, a presynaptic VGCC antibody disorder. LEMS is frequently paraneoplastic, so CT chest to detect small-cell lung cancer is the priority next step.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: Which statement about the electrophysiological evaluation of neuromuscular junction disorders is correct?
options: High-frequency stimulation is the standard screening test for myasthenia gravis
A normal low-frequency RNS study reliably excludes ocular myasthenia gravis
Single-fibre EMG is the most sensitive test but is not specific for a particular cause
LEMS produces a decremental response on low-frequency stimulation and no facilitation
Cooling the limb increases the sensitivity of the decrement in MG
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.answer: Single-fibre EMG is the most sensitive test but is not specific for a particular cause
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: Single-fibre EMG detects increased jitter and is the most sensitive test for an NMJ transmission defect, though increased jitter also occurs in other neuromuscular disease so it is not specific. Low-frequency RNS is the MG screen and may be normal in ocular disease, while LEMS shows increment, not decrement.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: What physiological parameter does single-fibre EMG primarily quantify?
options: The conduction velocity of the fastest motor axons
The amplitude decrement of the compound muscle action potential on repetitive stimulation
The number of motor units recruited during maximal contraction
The resting membrane potential of the muscle fibre
The variability in the interpotential interval between two muscle fibres of the same motor unit (jitter)
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.answer: The variability in the interpotential interval between two muscle fibres of the same motor unit (jitter)
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: SFEMG isolates two fibres from one motor unit and measures jitter, the discharge-to-discharge variability in their firing interval. This variability reflects fluctuation in neuromuscular synaptic delay and rises when the safety factor of transmission falls.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: A patient with ptosis and diplopia has normal repetitive nerve stimulation and negative acetylcholine-receptor antibodies, but SFEMG of orbicularis oculi shows markedly increased jitter with blocking. What is the best interpretation?
options: The findings exclude a neuromuscular junction disorder
The findings confirm a defect of neuromuscular transmission consistent with ocular myasthenia gravis
The findings are diagnostic of a primary myopathy
The result is a technical artefact and should be ignored
The result proves the patient has motor neurone disease
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.answer: The findings confirm a defect of neuromuscular transmission consistent with ocular myasthenia gravis
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: SFEMG is more sensitive than RNS and antibody testing and is frequently the only positive test in ocular or seronegative MG. Increased jitter with blocking demonstrates unstable NMJ transmission that fits the clinical picture of ocular myasthenia.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: Which statement best describes the specificity of an abnormal SFEMG result?
options: Increased jitter is specific for myasthenia gravis and confirms the diagnosis alone
Increased jitter only ever occurs in Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
Jitter is normal in all neurogenic disorders
Increased jitter is non-specific and also occurs in LEMS, motor neurone disease, neuropathies and myopathies
Blocking is seen exclusively in healthy muscle
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.answer: Increased jitter is non-specific and also occurs in LEMS, motor neurone disease, neuropathies and myopathies
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: Increased jitter signals any unstable neuromuscular transmission, not myasthenia specifically. Because it is raised in LEMS, botulism, motor neurone disease, neuropathies, myopathies and reinnervation, the result must be combined with clinical and antibody data.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: A 28-year-old woman with suspected MS has normal acuity and fundoscopy. VEP shows a markedly delayed P100 in the right eye with preserved amplitude. What does this indicate?
options: Demyelination of the right optic nerve
Axonal loss from ischaemic optic neuropathy
A lesion of the occipital cortex
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.answer: Demyelination of the right optic nerve
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: A delayed P100 with preserved amplitude is the signature of demyelination, which slows conduction while sparing axons. In this context it reflects previous or subclinical optic neuritis, supporting a diagnosis of MS.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: Which VEP finding best distinguishes demyelination from axonal loss?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: Demyelination slows conduction, prolonging latency while leaving axons and amplitude largely intact. Axonal loss instead reduces amplitude with relatively preserved latency.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: A patient has a delayed P100 on VEP. Which statement is correct about its interpretation?
options: It is diagnostic of multiple sclerosis on its own
It proves an acute, currently active lesion
It excludes any compressive optic nerve cause
It reflects a primary occipital cortex lesion
It confirms optic nerve demyelination but is not specific to MS
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.answer: It confirms optic nerve demyelination but is not specific to MS
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: A delayed P100 indicates demyelination of the optic nerve but the same pattern occurs in other optic neuropathies and compressive lesions. It contributes evidence toward MS without being diagnostic alone, and it can persist long after recovery.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: A 7-year-old has frequent brief staring episodes with eyelid flutter. During hyperventilation at EEG she has a typical event. What EEG pattern is expected?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: Childhood absence epilepsy produces generalised, symmetrical 3Hz spike-and-wave discharges. Hyperventilation is the classic activation manoeuvre that provokes the discharges and clinical absences.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: A 62-year-old presents with fever, confusion and seizures. EEG shows periodic lateralised epileptiform discharges over the temporal region. Which diagnosis does this most strongly suggest?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: HSV encephalitis has a predilection for the temporal lobes, and temporal PLEDs are the classic EEG correlate. The febrile encephalopathic presentation with focal temporal discharges fits HSV encephalitis, warranting urgent aciclovir.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: A 68-year-old has rapidly progressive dementia and startle myoclonus. EEG shows periodic sharp-wave complexes at about 1Hz. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus and periodic sharp-wave complexes at ~1Hz is the classic EEG picture of sporadic CJD. This pattern, alongside supportive MRI and CSF markers, supports the diagnosis.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: A patient with an ascending flaccid paralysis has a demyelinating pattern on nerve conduction studies. Which treatment is appropriate?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: Guillain-Barré syndrome is treated with IVIG or plasma exchange; corticosteroids are NOT effective. Serial FVC must be monitored for neuromuscular respiratory failure, with escalation to ITU/ventilation as needed.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.question: Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a decremental response, confirming myasthenia gravis. Besides acetylcholine-receptor antibodies, which investigation is most important?
options: Nerve conduction velocity of the sural nerve
CT/MRI of the thymus to look for a thymoma
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.answer: CT/MRI of the thymus to look for a thymoma
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__N.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma (~10–15%) and thymic hyperplasia, so imaging the mediastinum (CT/MRI thymus) is a key next step; thymoma is resectable. Anti-AChR (then anti-MuSK if negative) antibodies are also sent.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A 19-year-old presents with fever, neck stiffness and photophobia. LP shows turbid CSF, 2000 neutrophils/mm3, protein 2.1 g/L, CSF glucose 1.2 mmol/L with paired serum glucose 6.0 mmol/L. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Bacterial meningitis
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: Turbid fluid with a marked neutrophil pleocytosis, high protein and a CSF:serum glucose ratio of 0.2 (<0.5) is the classic pyogenic picture. Neutrophils plus low glucose define bacterial meningitis.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: CSF from a patient shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, protein 4.0 g/L and a very low glucose, with a fibrin web forming in the sample. Which diagnosis fits best?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Tuberculous meningitis
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: Lymphocytes with very high protein, very low glucose and a fibrin web are characteristic of TB meningitis. The low glucose separates it from viral meningitis, which shows normal glucose.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: Which single CSF finding most reliably distinguishes viral meningitis from tuberculous meningitis, given both show a lymphocytic pleocytosis?
options: A normal CSF glucose in viral versus a low glucose in TB
A clear appearance of the fluid
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: A normal CSF glucose in viral versus a low glucose in TB
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: Both viral and TB meningitis are lymphocytic, so cell type does not separate them. CSF glucose is the discriminator: normal in viral, markedly reduced in TB.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A patient presents with a thunderclap headache and has a negative CT head. When should the lumbar puncture ideally be performed to reliably detect xanthochromia?
options: At least 12 hours after headache onset
At exactly 48 hours regardless of onset
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: At least 12 hours after headache onset
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: Bilirubin is formed by the in-vivo breakdown of haemoglobin, a process that takes time. Delaying the LP to at least 12 hours after onset ensures enough bilirubin has formed for detection.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: Which CSF finding best distinguishes a genuine subarachnoid haemorrhage from a traumatic lumbar puncture?
options: Presence of bilirubin (xanthochromia) in the supernatant
Red cells in the first bottle
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Presence of bilirubin (xanthochromia) in the supernatant
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: Bilirubin forms only in vivo and so indicates blood that was present in the subarachnoid space, confirming SAH. A traumatic tap introduces fresh blood with no bilirubin and shows a falling red-cell count between bottles.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: What is the recommended laboratory method for confirming xanthochromia in suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage?
options: Holding the tube against a white card by eye
Counting red cells in a haemocytometer
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Spectrophotometry of the supernatant
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: Spectrophotometry measures net bilirubin absorbance across the visible spectrum and detects small amounts reliably. It outperforms subjective visual inspection and separates bilirubin from oxyhaemoglobin and other interferents.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A 30-year-old woman with a first episode of optic neuritis has CSF and serum sent for oligoclonal bands by isoelectric focusing. Which result best supports a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis?
options: No bands detected in either CSF or serum
Identical bands present in both CSF and serum
A single faint band shared by CSF and serum
Bands present in serum only, not in CSF
Two or more bands in CSF that are absent from the paired serum
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Two or more bands in CSF that are absent from the paired serum
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: CSF-restricted bands (present in CSF but absent from serum) demonstrate intrathecal IgG synthesis, the finding that supports MS. Bands shared with serum reflect a systemic process, and absent bands do not support the diagnosis.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: The IgG index is calculated from paired CSF and serum samples. Which value indicates raised intrathecal IgG production?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: IgG index greater than 0.7
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: The IgG index corrects CSF IgG for serum IgG and for blood-brain barrier integrity using albumin ratios. A value above 0.7 quantitatively indicates intrathecal IgG production consistent with a CNS inflammatory process such as MS.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A patient's CSF shows oligoclonal bands. Why is finding the same bands in the paired serum important to note?
options: It confirms the bands are due to multiple sclerosis
It proves an active CNS infection is present
It means the isoelectric focusing gel was faulty
It indicates a systemic rather than intrathecal source, arguing against MS
It quantifies the degree of demyelination
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: It indicates a systemic rather than intrathecal source, arguing against MS
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: Bands mirrored in both CSF and serum reflect systemic immune activation with immunoglobulin crossing into CSF, not local production. Only bands unique to the CSF indicate intrathecal synthesis and support MS.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A 34-year-old man develops ascending weakness and areflexia two weeks after a diarrhoeal illness. Which CSF pattern most supports Guillain-Barré syndrome?
options: Raised protein with a normal white cell count
Raised protein with a raised white cell count
Raised protein with low glucose and organisms on Gram stain
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Raised protein with a normal white cell count
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: GBS classically produces albuminocytological dissociation: elevated CSF protein with a normal cell count. This reflects inflammation of the nerve roots increasing protein leak without a cellular infiltrate.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A patient with suspected GBS has a lumbar puncture on day 3 of symptoms showing normal protein and normal cell count. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: GBS is excluded and an alternative diagnosis must be found
A normal early CSF does not exclude GBS; protein often rises after 1–2 weeks
The lumbar puncture must have been technically inadequate
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: A normal early CSF does not exclude GBS; protein often rises after 1–2 weeks
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: CSF protein may be normal in the first week of GBS and typically rises after 1–2 weeks. With a strong clinical picture, management should proceed and the lumbar puncture can be repeated later.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A patient with suspected GBS has CSF showing raised protein but a white cell count of 60 cells/mm³. What does the elevated cell count most appropriately prompt?
options: Immediate confirmation of the GBS diagnosis
Reassurance that this is the expected GBS pattern
Investigation for infection, malignant infiltration, or HIV
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Investigation for infection, malignant infiltration, or HIV
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: A raised CSF cell count argues against GBS, in which the count should be normal. Pleocytosis should prompt investigation for infection, malignant meningitis, or HIV seroconversion.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A 28-year-old obese woman has headache, papilloedema and blurred vision. CT and MRI are normal. At LP in the lateral decubitus position the opening pressure is 34 cmH₂O and CSF constituents are normal. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: An opening pressure >25 cmH₂O with normal imaging and normal CSF in an obese young woman with papilloedema is diagnostic of IIH. Draining CSF at the same LP also lowers the pressure therapeutically.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: Which opening pressure value is within the accepted normal adult range?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: 14 cmH₂O
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: The normal adult CSF opening pressure is 6–20 cmH₂O, so 14 cmH₂O is normal. Values below 6 suggest hypotension/leak and values above 25 suggest raised intracranial pressure.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A 74-year-old man has progressive gait apraxia, cognitive decline and urinary incontinence with ventriculomegaly on MRI. What best supports a diagnosis of normal-pressure hydrocephalus at LP?
options: A normal opening pressure with objective gait improvement after large-volume CSF removal
A markedly raised CSF white cell count
A CSF glucose below half the serum value
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: A normal opening pressure with objective gait improvement after large-volume CSF removal
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: NPH characteristically has a normal opening pressure, and the diagnosis is supported by measurable gait improvement after a large-volume tap. This response also predicts benefit from shunt insertion.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A 40-year-old with fever, confusion and a seizure has a lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose. What is the most important immediate action?
options: Await the PCR result before treating
Start IV ceftriaxone alone and observe
Start empirical IV aciclovir and send CSF HSV PCR
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Start empirical IV aciclovir and send CSF HSV PCR
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: Fever, encephalopathy/seizures and a lymphocytic CSF suggest HSV encephalitis, which has high mortality if untreated. Start empirical IV aciclovir immediately and send CSF HSV PCR; do not wait for the result.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A 68-year-old has a turbid CSF with neutrophils, high protein and low glucose. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
options: IV ceftriaxone plus amoxicillin (for Listeria) and dexamethasone
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: IV ceftriaxone plus amoxicillin (for Listeria) and dexamethasone
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: This is bacterial meningitis. Empirical IV ceftriaxone is given, with added amoxicillin for Listeria cover in those 60 or over, immunocompromised or pregnant, plus IV dexamethasone. Antibiotics must not be delayed for the LP.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A 62-year-old man develops progressive cognitive decline over 8 weeks with prominent startle-induced myoclonus. CSF is sent for prion diagnostics. Which finding is MOST specific for Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Positive CSF RT-QuIC
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: RT-QuIC directly detects misfolded prion protein by seeded aggregation and is highly specific (>98%) for CJD, making it a diagnostic criterion. The other findings are non-specific and 14-3-3 in particular rises in many causes of rapid neuronal loss.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A CSF 14-3-3 protein result returns positive. Which statement best explains its diagnostic limitation?
options: It is only positive in variant, not sporadic, CJD
It becomes positive only at end-stage disease
It requires brain biopsy to interpret
It is falsely lowered by blood contamination
It is also raised in stroke, encephalitis and other acute neuronal injury
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: It is also raised in stroke, encephalitis and other acute neuronal injury
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: 14-3-3 is a marker of rapid neuronal destruction and is therefore released in stroke, viral encephalitis, hypoxia and status epilepticus. This poor specificity means a positive result supports but cannot confirm CJD.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: When performing a lumbar puncture and handling instruments in a patient with suspected CJD, which precaution is MOST important?
options: Standard autoclaving of reusable instruments is sufficient
Use single-use instruments and follow prion-specific decontamination guidance
No special handling is needed as CJD is not transmissible
Antiviral prophylaxis for staff should be given
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Use single-use instruments and follow prion-specific decontamination guidance
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: Prions resist routine autoclaving, formalin and standard sterilisation, so single-use instruments and national prion decontamination protocols are required. CJD is transmissible, and CSF should be labelled as high-risk.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A 40-year-old presents with fever, confusion, dysphasia and a seizure. HSV encephalitis is suspected. What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?
options: Await the CSF HSV PCR result before starting any antiviral
Start oral valaciclovir and discharge with review
Withhold treatment until MRI is performed
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Start empirical IV aciclovir immediately
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: HSV encephalitis is a treatable emergency where every hour of delay increases mortality and disability. Empirical IV aciclovir is started on clinical suspicion, and the CSF PCR serves only to confirm the diagnosis afterwards.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A patient with strong clinical and MRI features of HSV encephalitis has a CSF HSV PCR taken 18 hours after symptom onset that returns negative. What is the correct interpretation and action?
options: An early negative PCR does not exclude HSE; continue aciclovir and repeat the PCR
HSV encephalitis is excluded; stop aciclovir
The lumbar puncture must have been technically failed
Switch to oral aciclovir as the risk is now low
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: An early negative PCR does not exclude HSE; continue aciclovir and repeat the PCR
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: Viral DNA may be undetectable in the first 24–72 hours, giving false-negative PCR results. With ongoing clinical suspicion, aciclovir is continued and the PCR is repeated after 72 hours to a week.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: Which CSF pattern is most consistent with herpes simplex encephalitis?
options: Neutrophilic pleocytosis with very low glucose and very high protein
Acellular CSF with markedly low glucose
Lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose and mildly raised protein
High neutrophils with normal protein and normal glucose
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose and mildly raised protein
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: HSV encephalitis produces a viral CSF picture of lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly to moderately raised protein and normal glucose. Red cells may also be seen owing to the haemorrhagic temporal-lobe necrosis, whereas low glucose with neutrophils points to bacterial infection.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A 22-year-old with excessive daytime sleepiness and episodes of knee-buckling triggered by laughter has an equivocal MSLT. CSF orexin-A is measured at 55 pg/mL. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Narcolepsy type 1
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: A CSF orexin-A ≤ 110 pg/mL is diagnostic of narcolepsy type 1. The emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone describes cataplexy, the clinical hallmark of type 1.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: Which HLA allele is most strongly associated with narcolepsy type 1?
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: HLA-DQB1*06:02
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: Narcolepsy type 1 shows a very strong association with HLA-DQB1*06:02, consistent with an autoimmune mechanism destroying orexin neurons. This underlies the low CSF orexin that defines the condition.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: In the diagnostic work-up of suspected narcolepsy, when is CSF orexin-A measurement most appropriately used?
options: As the first-line screening test for all daytime sleepiness
To monitor response to stimulant therapy
When the MSLT result is equivocal or unreliable
As a routine test before starting any sedative
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: When the MSLT result is equivocal or unreliable
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: CSF orexin measurement is invasive and reserved for cases where the MSLT is equivocal or cannot be reliably interpreted. The MSLT with prior polysomnography remains the usual first-line investigation.

investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.question: A 22-year-old is diagnosed with narcolepsy type 1 after a low CSF orexin and positive MSLT. Besides referral to sleep medicine, which advice is essential?
options: Advise not to drive and to notify the DVLA until symptoms are controlled
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.answer: Advise not to drive and to notify the DVLA until symptoms are controlled
investigations__NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__C.explanation: Excessive daytime sleepiness impairs driving safety, so a patient with symptomatic narcolepsy must be advised not to drive and to notify the DVLA until symptoms are controlled. Management otherwise includes modafinil for sleepiness and sodium oxybate for cataplexy.
